# Setup

## Runtime and installation

Requires Node.js 24.15+ (or 22.22.2+) and npm 12.2.1+. Check `node --version`,
`npm --version` and the resolved executable paths before changing anything.
The marketplace installs skill files, not npm packages.

On Windows, check `Get-Command nvm -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`, `nvm version` and
`nvm list`. With [nvm-windows](https://github.com/nvm-windows/nvm), reuse a
compatible installed version, or pick a supported LTS from `nvm list available`
and run `nvm install <version>` and `nvm use <version>` (switching may need
elevation). Never install a competing standalone Node or remove other versions.
Recheck `Get-Command node,npm`, `where.exe node` and versions afterwards. On
macOS/Linux reuse the user's version manager; nvm-sh commands differ.

Upgrade an old npm with `npm install --global npm@latest` using the selected Node.
On access denied, EPERM/EACCES or an elevation requirement, explain the failing
operation and give exact commands for the user's own terminal opened with **Run as
administrator**, selecting the same nvm version first. Do not retry repeatedly,
change ACLs, bypass execution policy or switch administrator accounts. `npm.cmd`
works if only the PowerShell npm wrapper is blocked. Recheck versions afterwards;
reopen the terminal/IDE if PATH is stale. Index without elevation.

Install dependencies in the installed skill directory (containing SKILL.md and
package.json), preserving its `.npmrc` and lockfile, then build:

```text
npm ci --prefix "<skill>"
node "<skill>/scripts/doktimoi.mjs" build "<folder>"
```

Indexed: `.md`, `.markdown`, `.txt`, `.text`, `.rst`, `.adoc`, `.asciidoc`, `.docx`,
`.doc`, `.xlsx`, `.xls`, `.pptx`, `.pdf`, `.html`/`.htm`, `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`,
`.webp`, `.drawio`/`.drawio.xml`, `.mmd`, `.svg`, `.csv`, `.tsv`, `.yaml`/`.yml` and
`.json`. Symlinks, hidden paths, dependency/build directories and ignored files are
skipped; in Git repositories only tracked or non-ignored files are used. Unsupported
formats and conversion warnings are reported; a failed conversion aborts the
query. Source files are never changed. For a tiny folder, reading sources directly
may be cheaper; decide by content volume and question, not file count.

Use the same quoted commands in PowerShell, macOS or Linux, with Windows paths such
as `"C:\Docs\Product"`; Bash and Python are not required. Legacy `.doc` (and images
in legacy `.xls`) need LibreOffice; if it is not in the standard Windows/macOS
location, set `DOKTIMOI_SOFFICE` to the executable path (`soffice.exe` on Windows).
Without it such files are skipped with a warning; run `build` after installing it.
Microsoft Office is not used.

OCR (`DOKTIMOI_OCR_LANGUAGES`, default `eng+fin`) downloads recognition data on
first use, then runs locally; `DOKTIMOI_OCR_CACHE` selects its cache. `DOKTIMOI_OCR`
is `auto` (images, embedded Office images and PDF pages with raster images or no
text), `always` (also native-text PDF pages) or `off`. Each format's limits (OCR
errors, charts, layout, unevaluated includes or aliases, extracted-line
citations) are reported as extraction warnings with its results; do not claim
complete coverage after one. Linked external resources are never fetched.

## Ask about the local AI option

During initial setup, ask whether to enable **local semantic search**, explaining
first in the user's language:

- Keyword search already works without a language model and suits exact names,
  codes and terms at low startup cost.
- Semantic search downloads QMD's embedding model (a few hundred MB), turns
  passages and questions into vectors locally and combines meaning with keywords.
  It helps paraphrases and Finnish/English cross-language questions but costs
  disk, RAM and indexing/startup time.
- It does not generate answers or guarantee correct matches. There is no cloud AI
  charge; the assistant still answers with its normal model and may send selected
  passages to that provider. OCR is separate.

Offer “Enable local semantic search” and “Keep keyword search” and recommend one
by corpus and language needs. Never opt in silently or treat silence as consent;
an explicit user request to enable embeddings is consent. Lexical indexing can
proceed meanwhile, but do not run `embed`, download a model or run hybrid search
before consent. Respect a recorded choice; ask again only if the user wants to
change it. After acceptance:

```text
node "<skill>/scripts/doktimoi.mjs" embed "<folder>"
```

Record semantic search as enabled only after it completes. On failure, report it,
keep keyword search and record enablement as pending; never present lexical
results as semantic. Afterwards use `--mode hybrid` for meaning-based questions
and keyword search for exact identifiers. Documents are never uploaded. Models
use QMD's local cache (`XDG_CACHE_HOME` isolates it); `QMD_FORCE_CPU=1` forces
CPU when Metal/CUDA is unavailable; report the mode when benchmarking.

## Turn semantic search on or off; check status

To turn it on later, ask for consent as above, then run `embed`. To turn it off
when the user asks (no consent question needed), run:

```text
node "<skill>/scripts/doktimoi.mjs" disable-semantic "<folder>"
```

It stops the folder's background server, removes the embeddings and keeps the
keyword index, so no rebuild is needed and no model or server starts again for
the folder. Then set the recorded choice in the doktimoi block to `keyword only`.
The model files stay in QMD's cache for other folders.

To see what the index and its background work are doing, run:

```text
node "<skill>/scripts/doktimoi.mjs" status "<folder>"
```

It changes and starts nothing: it reports source, chunk and warning counts, the
last index update, whether semantic search is on (and chunks still waiting for
embeddings), an interrupted update, whether the index lock is held, and the
background server: its process, plugin version, model state, current request and
idle exit time. Report it to the user in plain words.

## Future sessions

Append `.doktimoi/` to the folder's `.gitignore` once, preserving its content and
tracked files. Pick the first existing instruction file:

1. `AGENTS.md` (or an existing `Agents.md`).
2. `CLAUDE.md`.
3. `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, then a root `copilot-instructions.md`.

Read it and respect it and its recorded search choice unless higher-priority
instructions differ. If its `doktimoi:start` block differs from the one below,
replace the block with the current text, keep the recorded choice and tell the
user. Append or update only Doktimoi's block there; never copy it into a new
host-specific file or create AGENTS.md when another file exists. If several case
variants exist, report conflicts instead of choosing. Respect the `applyTo` scope
of `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md` files; do not make one folder-wide.
If no file exists, propose the current host's (`AGENTS.md` for Codex, `CLAUDE.md`
for Claude, `.github/copilot-instructions.md` for Copilot) and create it only
after the user accepts; indexing works without it. Append this block once, with
`<choice>` set to `keyword only`, `semantic enabled` or `semantic enablement pending`:

```markdown
<!-- doktimoi:start -->
This folder is indexed by doktimoi. For every content lookup here, including fact
checks while editing or maintaining files, search first with the installed
doktimoi skill, not Grep or whole-file reads. Use Grep only for file names or exact
edit locations in a file doktimoi already returned. Run each doktimoi search as a
single command without cd or chaining. Retrieve cited originals; do not load
.doktimoi machine indexes.
Local AI search choice: <choice>. Do not enable embeddings without consent.
<!-- doktimoi:end -->
```

Preserve all other content. Reject symlinked instruction or ignore files. Report
incomplete or duplicated markers instead of replacing unrelated content. If the
user declines the instructions, report the mode without claiming it will be
remembered. Do not write global host settings, commit, push or index linked
repositories during setup.

## Cache

`.doktimoi/` holds QMD's `index.sqlite`, `manifest.json` (source hashes and
locations), `chunks/` and `visuals/` (normalized images and rendered PDF pages);
it costs disk, not context. Searches rescan metadata, reconvert only changed
files, update embeddings when a semantic index exists and never return evidence that does not match its source:
while another update holds the per-folder lock for over a second, a search answers
from the current index with a note and leaves out sources changed since (`--verify`
waits instead). The lock serializes index updates, which re-index only changed
chunks (a first build, `build` and an interrupted update rescan all); searches run
without it (the background server rescans only after a file change, or once a
minute). `build` rehashes every source, and the first search after a plugin update
that changes chunking reconverts every source once (unchanged passages keep their
embeddings). `build` output lists extraction warnings; `status` counts them and
search shows only those of returned sources.
The cache is disposable: if it is incompatible or incomplete, rebuild it while
preserving unrelated user files. A folder with semantic search may have a
background search server holding `index.sqlite` open; run
`node "<skill>/scripts/doktimoi.mjs" stop "<folder>"` before deleting the cache
(`build` stops it itself). Old v1 `matrix.json`/`.ai` files are ignored.
# Planning and case-fit analysis

Find the product overview and architecture by filename, heading or a targeted
search. Search each requirement or proposed capability separately (terms,
constraints, integrations, access control) so a popular topic cannot crowd out
another; alternate queries in one call describe the same intent. Retrieve the
smallest sufficient evidence, batch independent lookups in one tool call when
useful and reuse still-relevant evidence from the conversation.

## Gap analysis

Keep customer requirements, meeting notes, released capabilities and roadmap
items separate. Classify each requirement as:

- Supported: cite the current capability and its conditions.
- Requires configuration/integration: cite the extension mechanism and the
  remaining work.
- Documented gap: cite the explicit incompatibility or unsupported capability.
- Unknown: documentation is missing, ambiguous or conflicting; state what to
  verify. A failed search never proves lack of support.

Quote the decisive range, not whole documents, with limits, roles,
prerequisites, versions and exceptions. A planned feature is not released, and a
customer requirement is not evidence of support.

## Feature planning and source repositories

Map the feature to documented components, data ownership, integrations and
security rules. Keep repo URLs and code paths from excerpts: they show where to
inspect, not current code behavior. Cite the documentation and label proposals
as proposals. If the task requires implementation verification, read only the
relevant files with the host's read-only repository tools within the user's
scope; never clone or index every linked repository.

When references conflict, retrieve both and explain the conflict, preferring
explicit version/release scope over filenames or scores. The first four results
are not exhaustive: broaden only for unresolved requirements, then list the
remaining uncertainties.

Pod disruption budgets
The "intended" number of pods is computed from the `.spec.replicas` of the workload resource
that is managing those pods. The control plane discovers the owning workload resource by
examining the `.metadata.ownerReferences` of the Pod.

[Involuntary disruptions](#voluntary-and-involuntary-disruptions) cannot be prevented by PDBs; however they
do count against the budget.

Pods which are deleted or unavailable due to a rolling upgrade to an application do count
against the disruption budget, but workload resources (such as Deployment and StatefulSet)
are not limited by PDBs when doing rolling upgrades. Instead, the handling of failures
during application updates is configured in the spec for the specific workload resource.

It is recommended to set `AlwaysAllow` [Unhealthy Pod Eviction Policy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#unhealthy-pod-eviction-policy)
to your PodDisruptionBudgets to support eviction of misbehaving applications during a node drain.

This page shows how to configure liveness, readiness and startup probes for containers.

For more information about probes, see [Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes](/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes)

The [kubelet](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kubelet/) uses
liveness probes to know when to restart a container. For example, liveness
probes could catch a deadlock, where an application is running, but unable to
make progress. Restarting a container in such a state can help to make the
application more available despite bugs.

A common pattern for liveness probes is to use the same low-cost HTTP endpoint
as for readiness probes, but with a higher failureThreshold. This ensures that the pod
is observed as not-ready for some period of time before it is hard killed.

tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:167-202
How does a HorizontalPodAutoscaler work? > Algorithm details
Due to technical constraints, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
cannot exactly determine the first time a pod becomes ready when
determining whether to set aside certain CPU metrics. Instead, it
considers a Pod "not yet ready" if it's unready and transitioned to
ready within a short, configurable window of time since it started.
This value is configured with the `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-initial-readiness-delay`
flag, and its default is 30 seconds.
Once a pod has become ready, it considers any transition to
ready to be the first if it occurred within a longer, configurable time
since it started. This value is configured with the
`--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-cpu-initialization-period` flag, and its
default is 5 minutes.

The \\( currentMetricValue \over desiredMetricValue \\) base scale ratio is then
calculated, using the remaining pods not set aside or discarded from above.

If there were any missing metrics, the control plane recomputes the average more
conservatively, assuming those pods were consuming 100% of the desired
value in case of a scale down, and 0% in case of a scale up. This dampens
the magnitude of any potential scale.

Furthermore, if any not-yet-ready pods were present, and the workload would have
scaled up without factoring in missing metrics or not-yet-ready pods,
the controller conservatively assumes that the not-yet-ready pods are consuming 0%
of the desired metric, further dampening the magnitude of a scale up.

After factoring in the not-yet-ready pods and missing metrics, the
controller recalculates the usage ratio. If the new ratio reverses the scale
direction, or is within the tolerance, the controller doesn't take any scaling
action. In other cases, the new ratio is used to decide any change to the
number of Pods.

Note that the _original_ value for the average utilization is reported
back via the HorizontalPodAutoscaler status, without factoring in the
not-yet-ready pods or missing metrics, even when the new usage ratio is
used.

Additional Considerations
### DNS

Kubernetes clusters include a Domain Name System (DNS) service to provide translations from names
to IP addresses, for all Services and Pods. By default, the Kubernetes DNS service allows lookups
across all namespaces in the cluster.

In multi-tenant environments where tenants can access pods and other Kubernetes resources, or where
stronger isolation is required, it may be necessary to prevent pods from looking up services in other
Namespaces.
You can restrict cross-namespace DNS lookups by configuring security rules for the DNS service.
For example, CoreDNS (the default DNS service for Kubernetes) can leverage Kubernetes metadata
to restrict queries to Pods and Services within a namespace. For more information, read an
[example](https://github.com/coredns/policy#kubernetes-metadata-multi-tenancy-policy) of
configuring this within the CoreDNS documentation.

Webhook configuration > Reinvocation policy
* The number of additional invocations is not guaranteed to be exactly one.
* If additional invocations result in further modifications to the object, webhooks are not
  guaranteed to be invoked again.
* Webhooks that use this option may be reordered to minimize the number of additional invocations.
* To validate an object after all mutations are guaranteed complete, use a validating admission
  webhook instead (recommended for webhooks with side-effects).

Here is an example of a mutating webhook opting into being re-invoked if later admission plugins
modify the object:

```yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: MutatingWebhookConfiguration
webhooks:
- name: my-webhook.example.com
  reinvocationPolicy: IfNeeded
```

Mutating webhooks must be [idempotent](#idempotence), able to successfully process an object they have already admitted
and potentially modified. This is true for all mutating admission webhooks, since any change they can make
in an object could already exist in the user-provided object, but it is essential for webhooks that opt into reinvocation.

The `Retain` reclaim policy allows for manual reclamation of the resource.
When the PersistentVolumeClaim is deleted, the PersistentVolume still exists

1. Manually clean up the data on the associated storage asset accordingly.

concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md:67-81
The two sorts of pod isolation
By default, a pod is non-isolated for ingress; all inbound connections are allowed.
A pod is isolated for ingress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and
has "Ingress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for ingress.
When a pod is isolated for ingress, the only allowed connections into the pod are those from
the pod's node and those allowed by the `ingress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to
the pod for ingress. Reply traffic for those allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
The effects of those `ingress` lists combine additively.

Network policies do not conflict; they are additive. If any policy or policies apply to a given
pod for a given direction, the connections allowed in that direction from that pod is the union of
what the applicable policies allow. Thus, order of evaluation does not affect the policy result.

For a connection from a source pod to a destination pod to be allowed, both the egress policy on

Dealing with disruptions
of cluster (node) autoscaling may cause voluntary disruptions to defragment and compact nodes.
Your cluster administrator or hosting provider should have documented what level of voluntary
disruptions, if any, to expect. Certain configuration options, such as
[using PriorityClasses](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-priority-preemption/)
in your pod spec can also cause voluntary (and involuntary) disruptions.


## Pod disruption budgets

{{< feature-state for_k8s_version="v1.21" state="stable" >}}

Kubernetes offers features to help you run highly available applications even when you
introduce frequent voluntary disruptions.

As an application owner, you can create a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) for each application.
A PDB limits the number of Pods of a replicated application that are down simultaneously from
voluntary disruptions. For example, a quorum-based application would
like to ensure that the number of replicas running is never brought below the
number needed for a quorum. A web front end might want to
ensure that the number of replicas serving load never falls below a certain
percentage of the total.

Cluster managers and hosting providers should use tools which
respect PodDisruptionBudgets by calling the [Eviction API](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/#eviction-api)
instead of directly deleting pods or deployments.

For example, the `kubectl drain` subcommand lets you mark a node as going out of
service. When you run `kubectl drain`, the tool tries to evict all of the Pods on
the Node you're taking out of service. The eviction request that `kubectl` submits on
your behalf may be temporarily rejected, so the tool periodically retries all failed
requests until all Pods on the target node are terminated, or until a configurable timeout
is reached.

A PDB specifies the number of replicas that an application can tolerate having, relative to how
many it is intended to have.  For example, a Deployment which has a `.spec.replicas: 5` is
supposed to have 5 pods at any given time.  If its PDB allows for there to be 4 at a time,
then the Eviction API will allow voluntary disruption of one (but not two) pods at a time.

The group of pods that comprise the application is specified using a label selector, the same
as the one used by the application's controller (deployment, stateful-set, etc).

`topologySpreadConstraints` field > Spread constraint definition
- **maxSkew** describes the degree to which Pods may be unevenly distributed. You must
  specify this field and the number must be greater than zero. Its semantics differ
  according to the value of `whenUnsatisfiable`:

  - if you select `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`, then `maxSkew` defines the
    maximum permitted difference between the number of matching pods in the target
    topology and the _global minimum_
    (the minimum number of matching pods in an eligible domain or zero if the number of eligible domains is less than MinDomains).
    For example, if you have 3 zones with 2, 2 and 1 matching pods respectively,
    `MaxSkew` is set to 1 then the global minimum is 1.
  - if you select `whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway`, the scheduler gives higher
    precedence to topologies that would help reduce the skew.

- **minDomains** indicates a minimum number of eligible domains. This field is optional.
  A domain is a particular instance of a topology. An eligible domain is a domain whose
  nodes match the node selector.

  <!-- OK to remove this note once v1.29 Kubernetes is out of support -->
  {{< note >}}
  Before Kubernetes v1.30, the `minDomains` field was only available if the
  `MinDomainsInPodTopologySpread` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates-removed/)
  was enabled (default since v1.28). In older Kubernetes clusters it might be explicitly
  disabled or the field might not be available.
  {{< /note >}}

  - The value of `minDomains` must be greater than 0, when specified.
    You can only specify `minDomains` in conjunction with `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`.
  - When the number of eligible domains with match topology keys is less than `minDomains`,
    Pod topology spread treats global minimum as 0, and then the calculation of `skew` is performed.
    The global minimum is the minimum number of matching Pods in an eligible domain,
    or zero if the number of eligible domains is less than `minDomains`.
  - When the number of eligible domains with matching topology keys equals or is greater than
    `minDomains`, this value has no effect on scheduling.
  - If you do not specify `minDomains`, the constraint behaves as if `minDomains` is 1.

- **topologyKey** is the key of [node labels](#node-labels). Nodes that have a label with this key
	and identical values are considered to be in the same topology.
  We call each instance of a topology (in other words, a <key, value> pair) a domain. The scheduler
  will try to put a balanced number of pods into each domain.
	Also, we define an eligible domain as a domain whose nodes meet the requirements of
	nodeAffinityPolicy and nodeTaintsPolicy.

- **whenUnsatisfiable** indicates how to deal with a Pod if it doesn't satisfy the spread constraint:
  - `DoNotSchedule` (default) tells the scheduler not to schedule it.
  - `ScheduleAnyway` tells the scheduler to still schedule it while prioritizing nodes that minimize the skew.

- **labelSelector** is used to find matching Pods. Pods
  that match this label selector are counted to determine the
  number of Pods in their corresponding topology domain.
  See [Label Selectors](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#label-selectors)
  for more details.

- **matchLabelKeys** is a list of pod label keys to select the pods over which
  spreading will be calculated. The keys are used to lookup values from the pod labels,
  those key-value labels are ANDed with `labelSelector` to select the group of existing
  pods over which spreading will be calculated for the incoming pod. The same key is
  forbidden to exist in both `matchLabelKeys` and `labelSelector`. `matchLabelKeys` cannot
  be set when `labelSelector` isn't set. Keys that don't exist in the pod labels will be
  ignored. A null or empty list means only match against the `labelSelector`.

  With `matchLabelKeys`, you don't need to update the `pod.spec` between different revisions.
  The controller/operator just needs to set different values to the same label key for different
  revisions. The scheduler will assume the values automatically based on `matchLabelKeys`. For
  example, if you are configuring a Deployment, you can use the label keyed with
  [pod-template-hash](/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#pod-template-hash-label), which
  is added automatically by the Deployment controller, to distinguish between different revisions
  in a single Deployment.

  ```yaml
      topologySpreadConstraints:
          - maxSkew: 1
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
            whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
            labelSelector:
              matchLabels:
                app: foo
            matchLabelKeys:
              - pod-template-hash
  ```

  {{< note >}}
  The `matchLabelKeys` field is a beta-level field and enabled by default in 1.27. You can disable it by disabling the
  `MatchLabelKeysInPodTopologySpread` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/).
  {{< /note >}}

- **nodeAffinityPolicy** indicates how we will treat Pod's nodeAffinity/nodeSelector
  when calculating pod topology spread skew. Options are:
  - Honor: only nodes matching nodeAffinity/nodeSelector are included in the calculations.
  - Ignore: nodeAffinity/nodeSelector are ignored. All nodes are included in the calculations.

   terminating and finish processing open connections.  Some applications need to go beyond
   finishing open connections and need more graceful termination, for example, session draining
   and completion.

   Any endpoints that represent the terminating Pods are not immediately removed from
   EndpointSlices, and a status indicating [terminating state](/docs/concepts/services-networking/endpoint-slices/#conditions)

   Terminating endpoints always have their `ready` status as `false` (for backward compatibility

### Forced Pod termination {#pod-termination-forced}

{{< caution >}}
Forced deletions can be potentially disruptive for some workloads and their Pods.
{{< /caution >}}

the `--grace-period=<seconds>` option which allows you to override the default and specify your

How does a HorizontalPodAutoscaler work?
  CPU utilization for the Pod will not be defined and the autoscaler will
  not take any action for that metric. See the [algorithm details](#algorithm-details) section below
  for more information about how the autoscaling algorithm works.

- For per-pod custom metrics, the controller functions similarly to per-pod resource metrics,
  except that it works with raw values, not utilization values.

- For object metrics and external metrics, a single metric is fetched, which describes
  the object in question. This metric is compared to the target
  value, to produce a ratio as above. In the `autoscaling/v2` API
  version, this value can optionally be divided by the number of Pods before the
  comparison is made.

The common use for HorizontalPodAutoscaler is to configure it to fetch metrics from
{{< glossary_tooltip text="aggregated APIs" term_id="aggregation-layer" >}}
(`metrics.k8s.io`, `custom.metrics.k8s.io`, or `external.metrics.k8s.io`). The `metrics.k8s.io` API is
usually provided by an add-on named Metrics Server, which needs to be launched separately.
For more information about resource metrics, see
[Metrics Server](/docs/tasks/debug/debug-cluster/resource-metrics-pipeline/#metrics-server).

[Support for metrics APIs](#support-for-metrics-apis) explains the stability guarantees and support status for these
different APIs.

The HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller accesses corresponding workload resources that support scaling (such as Deployments
and StatefulSet). These resources each have a subresource named `scale`, an interface that allows you to dynamically set the
number of replicas and examine each of their current states.
For general information about subresources in the Kubernetes API, see
[Kubernetes API Concepts](/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/).

### Algorithm details

From the most basic perspective, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
operates on the ratio between desired metric value and current metric
value:

```math
\begin{equation*}
desiredReplicas = ceil\left\lceil currentReplicas \times \frac{currentMetricValue}{desiredMetricValue} \right\rceil
\end{equation*}
```

For example, if the current metric value is `200m`, and the desired value
is `100m`, the number of replicas will be doubled, since
\\( { 200.0 \div 100.0 } = 2.0 \\).  
If the current value is instead `50m`, you'll halve the number of
replicas, since \\( { 50.0 \div 100.0 } = 0.5 \\). The control plane skips any scaling
action if the ratio is sufficiently close to 1.0 (within a globally-configurable
tolerance, 0.1 by default).

When a `targetAverageValue` or `targetAverageUtilization` is specified,
the `currentMetricValue` is computed by taking the average of the given
metric across all Pods in the HorizontalPodAutoscaler's scale target.

Before checking the tolerance and deciding on the final values, the control
plane also considers whether any metrics are missing, and how many Pods
are [`Ready`](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-conditions).
All Pods with a deletion timestamp set (objects with a deletion timestamp are
in the process of being shut down / removed) are ignored, and all failed Pods
are discarded.

If a particular Pod is missing metrics, it is set aside for later; Pods
with missing metrics will be used to adjust the final scaling amount.

When scaling on CPU, if any pod has yet to become ready (it's still
initializing, or possibly is unhealthy) _or_ the most recent metric point for
the pod was before it became ready, that pod is set aside as well.

## Protect slow starting containers with startup probes {#define-startup-probes}

Sometimes, you have to deal with applications that require additional startup
time on their first initialization. In such cases, it can be tricky to set up
liveness probe parameters without compromising the fast response to deadlocks
that motivated such a probe. The solution is to set up a startup probe with the
same command, HTTP or TCP check, with a `failureThreshold * periodSeconds` long
enough to cover the worst case startup time.

So, the previous example would become:

```yaml
ports:
- name: liveness-port
  containerPort: 8080

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: liveness-port
  failureThreshold: 1
  periodSeconds: 10

startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: liveness-port
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 10
```

Thanks to the startup probe, the application will have a maximum of 5 minutes
(30 * 10 = 300s) to finish its startup.
Once the startup probe has succeeded once, the liveness probe takes over to
provide a fast response to container deadlocks.
If the startup probe never succeeds, the container is killed after 300s and
subject to the pod's `restartPolicy`.

How Kubernetes applies resource requests and limits {#how-pods-with-resource-limits-are-run}
- The CPU limit defines a hard ceiling on how much CPU time the container can use.
  During each scheduling interval (time slice), the Linux kernel checks to see if this
  limit is exceeded; if so, the kernel waits before allowing that cgroup to resume execution.
- The CPU request typically defines a weighting. If several different containers (cgroups)
  want to run on a contended system, workloads with larger CPU requests are allocated more
  CPU time than workloads with small requests.
- The memory request is mainly used during (Kubernetes) Pod scheduling. On a node that uses
  cgroups v2, the container runtime might use the memory request as a hint to set
  `memory.min` and `memory.low`.
- The memory limit defines a memory limit for that cgroup. If the container tries to
  allocate more memory than this limit, the Linux kernel out-of-memory subsystem activates
  and, typically, intervenes by stopping one of the processes in the container that tried
  to allocate memory. If that process is the container's PID 1, and the container is marked
  as restartable, Kubernetes restarts the container.
- The memory limit for the Pod or container can also apply to pages in memory backed
  volumes, such as an `emptyDir`. The kubelet tracks `tmpfs` emptyDir volumes as container
  memory use, rather than as local ephemeral storage.　When using memory backed `emptyDir`,

`.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable` is an optional field that specifies the maximum number
of Pods that can be unavailable during the update process. The value can be an absolute number (for example, 5)

rounding down. The value cannot be 0 if `.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge` is 0. The default value is 25%.

down further, followed by scaling up the new ReplicaSet, ensuring that the total number of Pods available
at all times during the update is at least 70% of the desired Pods.

that can be created over the desired number of Pods. The value can be an absolute number (for example, 5) or a
percentage of desired Pods (for example, 10%). The value cannot be 0 if `MaxUnavailable` is 0. The absolute number

rolling update starts, such that the total number of old and new Pods does not exceed 130% of desired
Pods. Once old Pods have been killed, the new ReplicaSet can be scaled up further, ensuring that the

## Prerequisites

Network policies are implemented by the [network plugin](/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/network-plugins/).
To use network policies, you must be using a networking solution which supports NetworkPolicy.
Creating a NetworkPolicy resource without a controller that implements it will have no effect.

## The two sorts of pod isolation

There are two sorts of isolation for a pod: isolation for egress, and isolation for ingress.
They concern what connections may be established. "Isolation" here is not absolute, rather it
means "some restrictions apply". The alternative, "non-isolated for $direction", means that no
restrictions apply in the stated direction. The two sorts of isolation (or not) are declared
independently, and are both relevant for a connection from one pod to another.

By default, a pod is non-isolated for egress; all outbound connections are allowed.
A pod is isolated for egress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and has
"Egress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for egress.
When a pod is isolated for egress, the only allowed connections from the pod are those allowed by
the `egress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to the pod for egress. Reply traffic for those
allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
The effects of those `egress` lists combine additively.

Limits are a different story. Both `cpu` and `memory` limits are applied by the kubelet (and
{{< glossary_tooltip text="container runtime" term_id="container-runtime" >}}),
and are ultimately enforced by the kernel. On Linux nodes, the Linux kernel
enforces limits with
{{< glossary_tooltip text="cgroups" term_id="cgroup" >}}.
The behavior of `cpu` and `memory` limit enforcement is slightly different.

`cpu` limits are enforced by CPU throttling. When a container approaches
its `cpu` limit, the kernel will restrict access to the CPU corresponding to the
container's limit. Thus, a `cpu` limit is a hard limit the kernel enforces.
Containers may not use more CPU than is specified in their `cpu` limit.

`memory` limits are enforced by the kernel with out of memory (OOM) kills. When
a container uses more than its `memory` limit, the kernel may terminate it. However,
terminations only happen when the kernel detects memory pressure. Thus, a
container that over allocates memory may not be immediately killed. This means
`memory` limits are enforced reactively. A container may use more memory than
its `memory` limit, but if it does, it may get killed.

{{< note >}}
There is an alpha feature `MemoryQoS` which attempts to add more preemptive
limit enforcement for memory (as opposed to reactive enforcement by the OOM
killer). However, this effort is
[stalled](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/a47155b340/keps/sig-node/2570-memory-qos#latest-update-stalled)
due to a potential livelock situation a memory hungry can cause.
{{< /note >}}

{{< note >}}
If you specify a limit for a resource, but do not specify any request, and no admission-time
mechanism has applied a default request for that resource, then Kubernetes copies the limit
you specified and uses it as the requested value for the resource.
{{< /note >}}

## Resource types

*CPU* and *memory* are each a *resource type*. A resource type has a base unit.
CPU represents compute processing and is specified in units of [Kubernetes CPUs](#meaning-of-cpu).
Memory is specified in units of bytes.
For Linux workloads, you can specify _huge page_ resources.
Huge pages are a Linux-specific feature where the node kernel allocates blocks of memory
that are much larger than the default page size.

For example, on a system where the default page size is 4KiB, you could specify a limit,
`hugepages-2Mi: 80Mi`. If the container tries allocating over 40 2MiB huge pages (a
total of 80 MiB), that allocation fails.

Because Pods represent processes running on nodes in the cluster, it is important to

accidentally or maliciously sent to an unintended destination, or is intercepted by a workload on
a compromised node.

Pod-to-pod communication can be controlled using [Network Policies](/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/),
which restrict communication between pods using namespace labels or IP address ranges.
In a multi-tenant environment where strict network isolation between tenants is required, starting
with a default policy that denies communication between pods is recommended with another rule that
allows all pods to query the DNS server for name resolution. With such a default policy in place,
you can begin adding more permissive rules that allow for communication within a namespace.
It is also recommended not to use empty label selector '{}' for namespaceSelector field in network policy definition,
in case traffic need to be allowed between namespaces.
This scheme can be further refined as required. Note that this only applies to pods within a single
control plane; pods that belong to different virtual control planes cannot talk to each other via
Kubernetes networking.

**Decision memo — revise before production approval.** The proposed fields provide useful controls, but they do not establish five-replica availability, successful request draining, or database durability. The recommendations below distinguish documented behavior from configuration choices and validation requirements. All citations are local paths relative to the supplied `docs/` directory.

1. **PDB, failures, drains, and updates.** `minAvailable: 5` does not guarantee five available replicas during node failure: involuntary disruptions cannot be prevented, although they count against the budget. During a drain using the Eviction API, the PDB constrains voluntary evictions; with six healthy replicas, one can be evicted before further evictions must wait. Direct deletions bypass this protection. Deployment rolling updates also bypass PDB enforcement, although unavailable rollout Pods count against the budget.

   Replace `maxUnavailable: 2`, which permits availability to fall to four, with `maxUnavailable: 1`, `maxSurge: 1`; consider zero unavailable if surge capacity permits. These constrain rollout behavior, not simultaneous failures.  
   Sources: `concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions.md:100-141`; `concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md:1189-1211`.

2. **Zone placement and outage tradeoffs.** Configure a Pod topology spread constraint selecting all API replicas, with `topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone` and `maxSkew: 1`. Correct node labels and eligible capacity are prerequisites. With three usable zones, this targets two replicas per zone.

   Under `DoNotSchedule`, skew limits the difference between the target domain’s matching-Pod count and the global minimum. `ScheduleAnyway` makes reducing skew a scheduling preference, allowing imbalance. An unavailable zone does not imply automatic redistribution: eligibility and remaining capacity matter. Explicit `minDomains: 3` makes the minimum zero when fewer than three domains are eligible, potentially blocking replacements in already populated zones. Choose strict spreading or degraded-zone scheduling deliberately. Losing two of six evenly spread replicas leaves four.  
   Source: `concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md:82-140`.

3. **Probes for slow startup.** Use a startup probe whose `failureThreshold × periodSeconds` covers measured worst-case initialization. Readiness and liveness probes begin only after startup succeeds. Exhausting startup failures kills the container, with restart governed by `restartPolicy`.

   Readiness should indicate whether the API can accept useful requests, including necessary database access; failed readiness removes the Pod from Service load-balancer backends without itself requiring restart. Use liveness for unrecoverable process failure, such as deadlock. Avoid making a temporary database outage a reason to restart every API replica. That separation is a design recommendation; probe semantics cannot establish that the application’s checks are correct.  
   Sources: `tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes.md:13-43`, `:311-347`.

4. **Termination and long requests.** The grace-period clock starts **before** `preStop`. The hook therefore consumes shutdown time; afterward the runtime normally sends SIGTERM to process 1. Image stop-signal configuration can alter that signal. Remaining processes receive SIGKILL when grace expires; an overlong hook receives only a small, one-off two-second extension.

   Endpoint updates happen concurrently with shutdown. Terminating endpoints are not immediately removed from EndpointSlices, but have `ready: false` for regular traffic; `serving` supports draining-aware consumers. Thirty seconds is not a request-completion guarantee. Measure hook duration, request duration, and routing propagation, then configure sufficient grace and application draining.  
   Sources: `reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1.md:1006-1008`; `concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md:560-640`.

5. **Resource requests, limits, and HPA prerequisites.** Set realistic CPU requests for every relevant container. Requests guide placement and CPU allocation under contention; they are not ceilings. CPU limits impose throttling, which can lengthen requests. Memory limits instead trigger reactive OOM enforcement: exceeding the limit may cause a process kill, not immediate throttling or guaranteed immediate termination.

   CPU-utilization HPA measures usage relative to requests. If relevant requests are missing from some containers, Pod utilization is undefined and HPA does not act on that metric. Inspect admitted Pod configuration: when a limit exists without a request or admission default, Kubernetes copies the limit into the request.  
   Sources: `concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md:15-66`, `:252-269`; `tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:89-102`.

6. **Why HPA differs from the raw ratio.** The basic calculation rounds up current replicas multiplied by current/desired metric value, but ignores terminating and failed Pods and sets aside missing metrics and relevant not-yet-ready CPU samples. Missing metrics are conservatively treated as 100% of target for downscaling and 0% for upscaling. Not-yet-ready Pods further dampen scale-up using 0%.

   If recalculation reverses direction or falls within tolerance, scaling stops. Default tolerance is 10%; readiness-delay and CPU-initialization windows default to 30 seconds and five minutes. Downscale stabilization selects the highest recommendation from the preceding five-minute default window. Reported utilization excludes these conservative adjustments, so status alone need not explain the action.  
   Sources: `tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:129-202`, `:213-218`.

7. **Least-privilege networking.** Establish default-deny ingress and egress, then allow only approved callers to the API, API connections to the database’s required port, DNS queries to the cluster resolver, and explicitly identified operational dependencies. Scope rules with appropriate Pod and namespace selectors.

   Ingress and egress isolation are independent. Policies combine additively: a restrictive policy cannot override an existing allow-all rule. For Pod-to-Pod communication, both source egress and destination ingress must permit the connection; allowed reply traffic is implicit. A NetworkPolicy-capable networking plugin is a prerequisite—creating policy objects alone has no effect. Validate actual resolver destinations and enforcement in this cluster.  
   Sources: `concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md:46-81`, `:224-232`; `concepts/security/multi-tenancy.md:208-225`.

8. **Secrets and Git.** Base64 is reversible encoding, not confidentiality; reject base64-only Secrets in Git. The documentation explicitly describes encoded credentials as “obscured but not secret.” Kubernetes Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd by default.

   Enable encryption at rest, apply least-privilege RBAC, and expose each Secret only to containers that require it. Review workload-creation permissions alongside direct Secret access: someone authorized to create Pods in a namespace can use that ability to read its Secrets, including indirectly through Deployment creation. Encryption at rest does not cure excessive API permissions or protect an encoded copy committed to Git.  
   Sources: `concepts/configuration/secret.md:32-48`, `:304-307`.

9. **Storage lifecycle and data retention.** A dynamically provisioned PV inherits its StorageClass reclaim policy, defaulting to `Delete`. Changing the class’s policy does not retroactively rewrite existing PVs; inspect and explicitly patch those PVs where needed.

   With `Retain`, deleting a PVC leaves its PV released and its data requiring manual reclamation. With supported `Delete` implementations, reclamation removes both the PV and backing storage. StatefulSet deletion or scale-down is a separate decision: claim retention defaults to `Retain`; optional `whenDeleted` and `whenScaled` policies can delete generated PVCs, subject to the documented feature prerequisite. PVC deletion then engages PV reclamation. Neither retention mechanism constitutes a backup.  
   Sources: `concepts/storage/storage-classes.md:126-135`; `concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md:185-210`; `concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset.md:387-425`.

10. **Prioritized rollout and validation checklist.** First, remove the credential-exposure pattern, enable encryption and scoped RBAC, verify network-policy enforcement, and inspect existing database PV policies. Second, implement probes and draining, resource requests, compatible rollout settings, and an explicit zone-outage placement choice. Third, validate metrics availability and configure HPA bounds consistent with the intended six-replica baseline; Metrics Server is normally a separately installed prerequisite.

   Before release, exercise a rolling update, node drain, zone outage, database interruption, long-request shutdown, and PVC lifecycle in a representative environment. Acceptance must establish at least these undocumented application-specific limits: worst-case startup time; request-drain completion time; surviving-zone and database capacity; and storage recovery/durability. Also test CPU throttling, OOM behavior, and HPA response under missing metrics. These tests turn configurable mechanisms into evidence for this deployment.  
   Sources: `tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md:113-118`; `concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions.md:126-135`; `concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md:611-640`; `concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md:185-210`.
